response.text:
The Pequod’s latter voyage slides from workaday whaling into omen and obsession, even as Ishmael keeps noting the cruel elegance of the craft: Stubb’s boat runs a sperm whale to a bloody flurry, its magical line burning wrists and smoking round a loggerhead, and the carcass is cut in by song, steel, and windlass until the head itself is hung alongside like a black Sphinx. In the cutting-in and the try-works, sharks frenzy through the night while Stubb jokes and dines on whale-steak, old Fleece preaches to the fish, and the crew harvests spermaceti, black bone, ambergris, and a thousand facts of cetology from heads, ribs, case and junk; yet Ahab leans over the severed brow and demands oracles from the mute thing. The Pequod meets the Jeroboam and hears, from fever-haunted Gabriel, that the White Whale is an untouchable god; meets the Jungfrau and another parade of empty bravado; and sails on into the Bashee Isles and the Japan grounds while Pip, abandoned in a moment of fear and then plucked from the abyss, loses his wits and becomes the ship’s cracked conscience. Night at the try-works turns the ship into a fire-ship and Ahab into a man who renounces instruments and charts, rails at the heavens, and resolves that dead-reckoning, not any human quadrant, will steer him to his quarry.

A typhoon blackens the world and coronas of St. Elmo’s fire crown the masts; Ahab baptizes his harpoon in the pagans’ blood and curses it in the devil’s name, while Starbuck pleads prudence and sees in every sign an omen the old man scorns. In calmer light, the carpenter and blacksmith hammer at bones and steel, fashioning Ahab’s spare leg and a new, infernal iron, while Pip nestles in the captain’s own chair and Ishmael muses how coffins and life-buoys may be one. When lightning spoils the binnacle needles Ahab mocks the gods by forging a new compass on deck, then orders Queequeg’s coffin—first shunned, then carved, then hooped and pitched—to be rigged as the ship’s life-buoy. Soon after, the Rachel rushes up with men crowding her yards and a Nantucket captain begging Ahab to help search for his lost twelve-year-old son; Ahab, torn for a heartbeat by thoughts of his own child, refuses, and the Rachel, weeping for her children, falls astern.

From that hour the Pequod seems bound in a spell: Starbuck, Stubb, Flask, and the pagan harpooneers move like extensions of Ahab’s will, while the Parsee Fedallah stands apart, silent and watchful, his prophecies of two hearses and hemp only worming into the captain’s mind. They fault the White Whale at last, and the first day’s lowering tangles lines and snaps lives; the second day, Moby Dick breaches like a snowy mountain and smashes boats while Fedallah vanishes, only to reappear lashed dead to the whale’s back. As dusk falls the third day dawns, Ahab clings to his purpose though Starbuck, at last near mutiny, begs him to turn for home; new oars are set, a fresh flag is nailed to the main-truck, and the old man promises gold and perdition in the same breath. The chase tightens, and in a swirl of foam and circling sharks the White Whale drives his forehead into the Pequod’s bow and then under her, holing the ship while the three masthead harpooneers keep their posts to the last.

Ahab harpoons his hate one final time, the line snarls round his neck, and he is jerked voiceless into the sea, from hell’s heart stabbing, from hell’s breath cursing, even as the ship founders. Tashtego, nailing the red flag to the sinking spar, snags a sky-hawk in the cloth and vanishes with mast and bird into the green vault, and then the sea rolls over and erases everything as if five thousand years had not passed. Alone afloat, Ishmael—who had earlier been named to take Fedallah’s place and then had been pitched aside by the whale’s violence—finds Queequeg’s coffin-buoy bursting up through the vortex and clings to it through a day and a night of lullaby swells, spared even by the sharks. In the end it is the Rachel, still combing the waste for her lost boy, that finds and saves another orphan.

Across these last waters, the book binds its whaling ledger to its gospel: technical rites of flensing and forging become sacraments in a faith of iron will, the ship a floating chapel and charnel, and Ahab’s monomania a theology of defiance that will not bow to storm, omen, or love. Starbuck’s prudence, Stubb’s gallows humor, Flask’s appetite, the pagan courage of Queequeg, Daggoo, and Tashtego, the Parsee’s fatal quiet, and Pip’s broken visions all gather under one nailed doubloon and one nailed flag and are carried down by one nailed fate. The sea, serene and murderous by turns, outlasts them all, a void where spouts look like cities at dawn and heads like temples at dusk, and where severed skulls offer no speech but draw the living on. When the great shroud rolls back into place and only a coffin floats, Ishmael’s survival feels less like an ending than a margin note: the sole witness borne up by friendship’s handiwork, left to measure, in cool prose and long digressions, how far a single will can drive a crew, a craft, and a world, and how small a plank is required to carry a man back into the human sight.
